drug_class: Biologic therapy / Anti-angiogenic monoclonal antibody (VEGF inhibitor)
purpose: Bevacizumab-awwb is used to treat several types of cancer, including colorectal cancer, lung cancer, kidney cancer, cervical cancer, and certain brain tumors. It is often used in combination with chemotherapy or other cancer medicines. It works by helping to slow or stop the growth of tumors.
how_it_works: Tumors need to grow new blood vessels to get the nutrients they need to survive and spread — this process is called angiogenesis. This medicine blocks a protein called VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor), which is like cutting off the tumor's blood supply. Without enough blood flow, the tumor has a harder time growing and spreading.
common_side_effects: High blood pressure, feeling tired or weak, headache, loss of appetite, nausea, diarrhea, constipation, runny nose, mouth sores, dry skin, and changes in your sense of taste. Your doctor will monitor you closely for these.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious problems including severe bleeding, wounds that won't heal properly, bowel perforations (holes in the intestine), blood clots, stroke, heart problems, and kidney damage (protein in urine). Tell your doctor right away if you have unusual bleeding, chest pain, sudden vision changes, severe headache, or signs of infection. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby. Effective birth control is very important during and after treatment.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as an IV infusion (drip into a vein) by a nurse or doctor at a clinic or infusion center. The dose and how often you get it depends on the type of cancer being treated — it is commonly given every 2 or 3 weeks. Your first infusion is given slowly over about 90 minutes; if you tolerate it well, later infusions may be shorter.
